clue.text: Have a little drink, man! Courage! Get addicted!

parts.note: to have something, such as a meal, is to take it
a tot is a small measure of spirits
he stands for a man
bottle is British slang for nerve or courage

explanation.surface: A string of exclamations urging a nervous man to take a nip for Dutch courage, ending in a warning.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation marks break the clue into separate shouts that turn out to be the four parts. BOTTLE meaning nerve is British slang ('he lost his bottle').
explanation.definitionFit: To start drinking heavily and habitually is an idiom for becoming dependent on alcohol.

clue.text: Man commonly said to be so when wearing kilt?

indicators.note: said in a common or careless accent, so the clue's description is a word heard rather than spelt

parts.note: a true Scotsman is said to wear nothing under his kilt, i.e. to go without underpants

explanation.surface: A jokey question about the old tradition of what a Scotsman wears under his kilt.
explanation.walkthrough: Said carelessly, 'knicker-less' (without knickers, British for underpants) becomes a man's first name. The question mark flags the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: A common male first name, so it can stand for a man.

clue.text: Girl about 13

indicators.note: about signals that the letters of the referenced answer are turned around and rearranged

parts.note: the answer to 13 across, a word for painting media

explanation.surface: A bare cross-reference, the girl's age given as 13.
explanation.walkthrough: '13' looks like the girl's age, but it is the answer to 13 across, whose letters 'about' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: A female first name, so it indicates a girl.

clue.text: Director of "The Apple Cart"?

parts.note: a Cox is a variety of English eating apple, read possessively as Cox's
a wain is an old word for a farm cart or wagon

explanation.surface: A question about who directed the George Bernard Shaw play The Apple Cart.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the play's title as 'the Cox's wain'. A Cox's Orange Pippin is a well-known British apple. The 'director' steers a rowing boat, not a stage play.
explanation.definitionFit: The cox of a rowing boat steers and directs the crew, so is a kind of director.

clue.text: Fascist worthy encircles south German forest (26's work)

indicators.note: encircles means the first piece is wrapped around what follows

parts.note: OM, the Order of Merit, is held by a distinguished person, a worthy
Wald is German for forest

indicators.note: work used as a verb means the letters are worked into a new order

parts.note: the answer to 26 across, the film director

explanation.surface: A notable British Fascist surrounding a German forest, with a nod to a film director's output.
explanation.walkthrough: '(26's work)' looks like a note about a film, but 'work' rearranges the letters of the 26-across answer to give OSLEY. The man named was the leader of the British Union of Fascists in the 1930s.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Oswald Mosley founded and led the British Union of Fascists, so he is the archetypal British Fascist.

clue.text: Quarters sound more friendly where branches are trained

parts.note: east and south are two of the four quarters, or compass points

indicators.note: sound signals that the next words are heard rather than spelt

parts.note: pallier, more pally, means more friendly

explanation.surface: Barracks that sound more welcoming, in a garden where branches are trained.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quarters' looks like lodgings; it gives two compass points, E and S. 'Pallier' (more pally) is heard as PALIER.
explanation.definitionFit: A trellis or framework on which fruit tree branches are trained flat; also the tree itself.

clue.text: The truth is what happens below

definitions.meaning: said to introduce a correction or actual state of affairs, meaning actually
what really takes place down here on earth, actually, as against in theory

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means actually or really, both as a sentence opener and as describing what truly happens.

clue.text: Spread white paint on gap for such an 18

indicators.note: spread means the letters are scattered and laid out in a new order

explanation.surface: Instructions for slapping white paint on a gap, risking some mishap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spread' looks like a painting instruction but is the anagram signal. An 18 (accident) that is bound to occur is called 'an accident waiting to happen'.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'an accident waiting to happen' describes a disaster that seems inevitable.

clue.text: Merops is the son of a Welshman with love for America

parts.note: ap is the Welsh patronymic meaning son of, as in ap Rhys
Ivor is a typically Welsh man's name
love is zero in tennis, which looks like the letter O
US is short for United States, America

explanation.surface: A genealogical note claiming that someone called Merops descends from a Welshman who loved America.
explanation.walkthrough: Merops is the genus name of the bee-eaters, which makes 'Merops' look like a person's name. The definition is the phrase 'Merops is ___'.
explanation.definitionFit: Bee-eaters (genus Merops) feed on bees, and the adjective means bee-eating.

clue.text: Could be Barbara, but if 20 (say) 2

parts.note: the Californian city named after a saint comes first; then the word in 20 down, said aloud, gives the Christmas gift-bringer, who is the saint named in 2 down

explanation.surface: A riddle about a word that may precede the name Barbara or, with a cross-referenced word, give a saint.
explanation.walkthrough: With Barbara it is the city in California; followed by a word sounding like the 20-down answer it is the Christmas figure, who is the 2-down saint, of Myra.
explanation.definitionFit: Spanish and Portuguese for saint, used in place names and in the name of Father Christmas.

clue.text: End of the matter invaded by males (erroneously?) — Syracusan twins?

indicators.note: end of means only the final letter of the next word is taken
invaded by means the first piece has the second piece pushed inside it

parts.note: matter is an old word for pus, as in a wound discharging matter
he's, plural of he, is a word for males

explanation.surface: A muddled note on Shakespeare's Comedy of Errors, with a pair of twins from Syracuse.
explanation.walkthrough: '(erroneously?)' points to The Comedy of Errors, where twins from Syracuse meet their identical counterparts living in this Greek city. 'Matter' here means pus, not subject.
explanation.definitionFit: In The Comedy of Errors, the Syracusan twins Antipholus and Dromio find their twin brothers in this city, hence the link.

clue.text: One giving birth to insect (this is much of 14)

parts.note: in Genesis Eve is made from Adam's rib, so Adam in a sense gave birth to her
an ant is an insect

explanation.surface: A birth notice for an insect, with a cross-reference to how tough someone is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One giving birth' looks like a mother, but it is the first man, from whose rib Eve was made.
explanation.definitionFit: Being unyielding is a large part of being tough and cynical, so this word covers much of the 14-across sense.

clue.text: Kin to waterproof in which to paint

indicators.note: kin added to the answer makes a waterproof, so taking the clue's kin away from that garment leaves the answer

parts.note: an oilskin is a waterproof coat made of oiled cloth
taken as written

explanation.surface: Relatives preparing to waterproof something before painting.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'Kin to waterproof' as 'add KIN to get a waterproof': the answer is OILSKIN without KIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Oil paints are a medium, and artists are said to paint in oils.

clue.text: Ruth absent from such (because birth 10 AD?)

indicators.note: because with the question mark suggests the letters of what follows explain the answer once rearranged

parts.note: ten written as a word

explanation.surface: A mock explanation of why Ruth is missing from a group: they were born in 10 AD.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruth absent' means ruthless; ruth is an old word for pity. The parenthesis rearranges BIRTH, TEN and AD.
explanation.definitionFit: A tough, cynical person is without pity, and ruth is an old word for pity, so ruthless.

clue.text: One 23 shaken by banshee

indicators.note: shaken means the letters of the next word are jumbled up

explanation.surface: Someone frightened by a wailing spirit from Irish folklore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One 23' reads with the 23-across answer as 'one that was', someone whose time is past.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone whose success is in the past is one that was, no longer what they were.

clue.text: Side roads for inserting words?

parts.note: an edge is a side
ways are roads, as in highways

explanation.surface: A suggestion that side roads exist for slipping in a word or two.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'get a word in edgeways' means managing to speak when someone else is talking nonstop.
explanation.definitionFit: In the idiom about squeezing a word in during someone's monologue, this is the manner of insertion.

clue.text: Insert first section of 26's film subject

definitions.meaning: a Losey film title lacks its opening word, which must be added to give The ___

explanation.definitionFit: Losey's 1963 film is The Servant, and a servant is subject to a master, so one in service.

clue.text: Hot day for reptile turning into female on river

indicators.note: into means the turned piece goes inside the female

parts.note: she refers to a female

indicators.note: turning means the word for the reptile is read backwards

parts.note: croc is short for crocodile, a reptile

explanation.surface: A crocodile changing sex on a river on a hot day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning' looks like the reptile changing sex, but it turns the reptile's word backwards; 'into female' then puts that inside the pronoun.
explanation.definitionFit: A very hot day is informally called a scorcher.

clue.text: 26's work by 2 21: who he is shows in how he talks

indicators.note: shows in means the identity piece appears inside the speech piece

parts.note: an accent is the way a person speaks
ID, identification, is who someone is

explanation.surface: A remark about a novelist whose identity is revealed by the way he speaks.
explanation.walkthrough: Accident is a 1965 novel by Nicholas Mosley, filmed by Joseph Losey in 1967, so it is both men's work.
explanation.definitionFit: The Losey film of 1967, adapted from Nicholas Mosley's novel, has this one-word title.

clue.text: No streaky game?

parts.note: streaky bacon is from the belly; bacon from the back, and gammon from the leg, is not streaky, and together the two words name a board game

explanation.surface: A question about a board game with no lucky streaks.
explanation.walkthrough: Back bacon and gammon are British cuts of pork that are not streaky, unlike bacon from the belly.
explanation.definitionFit: A board game for two played with dice and counters.

clue.text: Injurious sounding part of sentence

indicators.note: sounding means the injurious thing is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: claws are injurious, things that inflict wounds

explanation.surface: Part of a sentence that sounds harmful.
explanation.walkthrough: Things that do injury, claws, said aloud give a grammatical term.
explanation.definitionFit: A grammatical unit with its own verb, forming part of a sentence.

clue.text: See 5
First red card in Indonesia

parts.note: an ace counts as first, number one
H stands for hearts, a red suit of cards

explanation.surface: A footballer receiving the first red card in an Indonesian match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'red card' looks like football's sending-off; it is a card from a red suit. Aceh is a province at the northern tip of Sumatra.
explanation.definitionFit: Aceh is a province of Indonesia, on the northern tip of Sumatra.

clue.text: The unfinished, unbegun legal judgments either side of the week

indicators.note: unfinished means the word loses its last letter
unbegun means the word loses its first letter

parts.note: fatwas are rulings on points of Islamic law

explanation.surface: A lawyer's week bracketed by half-finished legal rulings.
explanation.walkthrough: The 1960s satirical BBC TV show 'That Was The Week That Was' has these words on either side of 'the week'.
explanation.definitionFit: In the TV title the same phrase stands before and after the words 'the week'.

clue.text: Knowing one's stuff — but when shall I do the downs?

definitions.text: when shall I do the downs?
definitions.meaning: a crossword solver who has clued the across entries is done with the acrosses and up to the downs

explanation.definitionFit: Being well informed and knowledgeable is the meaning of the informal idiom.

clue.text: Impulse for our generation

indicators.note: for here signals that the answer sits inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: A drive that belongs to our generation.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is the run of letters inside 'our generation'.
explanation.definitionFit: An urge is a strong impulse or desire to do something.

clue.text: Mislay unknown director

parts.note: to mislay something is to lose it
Y is a mathematical unknown, like x

explanation.surface: Losing track of an unknown film director.
explanation.walkthrough: Joseph Losey was an American film director who worked in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Joseph Losey directed The Servant, Accident and The Go-Between.

clue.text: Issue featuring men smitten with Greece

indicators.note: smitten means struck, so the letters are knocked into a new order

explanation.surface: An issue involving men in love with Greece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'smitten' looks like 'in love with' but signals the anagram of MEN and GREECE.
explanation.definitionFit: To issue from somewhere is to emerge, and the noun for coming out is a synonym of issue.
